# AF 第六章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 6

[P01] All that year the animals worked like slaves. But they were happy in their work. They gave every effort and sacrifice（牺牲）, because they knew all their work was for themselves and for the animals who would come after them, not for a group of lazy, thieving（偷窃） humans. All spring and summer they worked sixty hours a week. In August Napoleon said there would be work on Sunday afternoons too. This work was truly their own choice, but any animal who did not come would have his food cut by half.

[P02] Still, some work was left undone（毁掉）. The harvest was a little smaller than before. Two fields should have had roots in early summer, but the ploughing was not finished in time. They could see the winter would be hard. Any animal who did not come would have his food cut by half. The windmill（风车） brought problems they did not expect. There was a good quarry（采石场） of limestone（石灰石） on the farm, and plenty of sand and cement（水泥） in one outhouse（外屋）, so all the materials were close at hand.

[P03] But the first problem the animals could not solve was how to break the stone into right-sized pieces. They could only use picks and crowbars（铁撬）, and no animal could use those, because no animal could stand on two back legs. After weeks of useless（无用） work, someone got the right idea—to use gravity（重力）. Huge rocks lay all over the floor of the quarry. The animals tied ropes around them, and all together—cows, horses, sheep, any animal that could hold the rope, and even the pigs sometimes joined—they pulled them slowly up the slope（斜坡） to the top of the quarry. There they pushed them over the edge, and the rocks broke into pieces below.

[P04] Moving the stone after it was broken was easier. The horses pulled it away in carts, the sheep dragged（拖） single blocks, and even Muriel and Benjamin tied themselves to an old governess（女教师）-cart and did their part. By late summer they had piled up enough stone, and then the building began, led by the pigs. But it was a slow, hard process. Frequently it took a whole day of tiring work to drag one boulder（巨石） to the top of the quarry, and sometimes when it was pushed over the edge, it did not break.

[P05] Nothing could be done without Boxer. His strength seemed as great as all the other animals together. When the boulder slipped（滑倒） and the animals cried out as they were pulled down, Boxer always pulled hard on the rope and stopped it. They admired him as he worked up the slope inch by inch, breathing fast, his hoofs（蹄） digging into the ground, his sides wet with sweat（汗水）. Clover sometimes warned him to be careful and not work too hard, but Boxer never listened to her.

[P06] His two slogans, "I will work harder" and "Napoleon is always right," seemed a good answer to every problem. He asked the young rooster（公鸡） to wake him three-quarters（住处） of an hour earlier each morning. In his few free moments, he went alone to the quarry, gathered（聚集） broken stone, and pulled it to the windmill site（场地）. The animals were not too badly off that summer, though their work was hard. They had no more food than in Jones's day, but at least not less.

[P07] The good thing was that they only had to feed themselves, not five wasteful（浪费） humans. This was such a big gain that many failures（失败） would be needed to cancel it out. And the animals' way of working was better and saved work. Weeding（除草）, for example, could be done more completely than any human could. And since no animal stole now, they did not need to fence off the fields, which saved much work on hedges（树篱） and gates. Still, as the summer went on, unexpected（意外） shortages began to appear.

[P08] They needed paraffin（石蜡） oil (石蜡油), nails（钉子）, string, dog biscuits, and iron for the horses' shoes. None of these could be made on the farm. Later they would also need seeds and man-made manure（肥料）, as well as different tools and, in the end, the machines for the windmill. No one could imagine how to get these things. The good side of feeding only themselves, and not also five wasteful humans, was so big that many failures would be needed to cancel it out. One Sunday morning, the animals came together to get their orders. Napoleon said he had decided on a new plan.

[P09] From now on, Animal Farm would trade with the neighbouring farms, not for business, but only to get materials they had to have. The needs of the windmill must come first, he said. So he was getting ready to sell a stack（堆） of hay（干草） and part of this year's wheat, and later, if more money were needed, it would come from selling eggs, which always had a market in Willingdon. The hens, said Napoleon, should welcome this sacrifice as their gift towards building the windmill. Once again the animals felt a vague（模糊） uneasiness（不安）.

[P10] They had agreed never to deal with humans, never to trade, never to use money. Was this not one of the first rules passed at the great Meeting after they drove Jones out? All the animals remembered such rules, or thought they did. The four young pigs who had spoken up when Napoleon ended the Meetings now raised their voices in fear, but the dogs' tremendous（极大的） growling（咆哮） silenced them. Then the sheep started "Four legs good, two legs bad!" and the awkward（笨拙的） moment passed. At last Napoleon raised his trotter（猪蹄） for silence and said he had already made all the plans.

[P11] No animal would ever have to meet human beings, which was clearly very bad. He would carry the whole load（负载） himself. Whymper, a solicitor（律师） living in Willingdon, agreed to stand between Animal Farm and the outside world, and would come to the farm every Monday morning to get his orders. Napoleon ended with his usual cry of "Long live Animal Farm!" and after the song 'animals of England' the animals were sent away. Afterwards（后来） Squealer walked around the farm and made the animals feel calm.

[P12] He told them the resolution against trade and money had never been passed, or even suggested. It was pure imagination, probably from Snowball's lies. A few animals still felt doubtful（怀疑的）, but Squealer asked cleverly, "Are you certain this is not something you have dreamed, comrades（同志们）? Have you any record of such a resolution? Is it written down anywhere?" Every Monday Mr. Whymper visited the farm, and since nothing of the kind existed in writing, the animals were satisfied they had been mistaken. Every Monday Mr. Whymper visited the farm as arranged（安排）.

[P13] He was a sly（狡猾的） little man with side whiskers（胡须）. He was a lawyer with little business, but he saw before anyone else that Animal Farm would need a broker, and the commissions（佣金） would be worth having. The animals watched him with dread（恐惧）, and stayed away from him. Nevertheless, when they saw Napoleon on all fours giving orders to Whymper, who stood on two legs, they felt proud, and this partly made them accept the new arrangement. Their relations with humans were now not quite the same. The humans did not hate Animal Farm any less now that it was prospering（繁荣的）; in fact, they hated it more than ever.

[P14] Every human believed the farm would go bankrupt（破产） sooner or later, and above all, that the windmill would fail. They met in the public-houses and proved to one another with diagrams（图表） that the windmill was sure to fall down, or that if it did stand, it would never work. Yet, against their will, they had grown a certain respect for how well the animals managed their own affairs（事务）. One sign of this was that they had begun to call Animal Farm by its proper name and stopped pretending it was called the farm Farm.

[P15] They had also stopped supporting Jones. Jones had given up hope of getting his farm back and gone to live in another part of the county. Except through Whymper, there was still no contact between Animal Farm and the outside world. But people often said that Napoleon was going to make a business agreement either with Mr. Pilkington of Foxwood（狐林） or with Mr. Frederick of Pinchfield（窄地）—but never, people noticed, with both at the same time. It was about this time that the pigs suddenly moved into the farmhouse（农舍） and made it their home.

[P16] Again the animals seemed to remember a rule against this from long ago, and again Squealer convinced（确信） them it was not true. He said the pigs, the brains of the farm, needed a quiet place to work. It also suited the dignity（尊严） of the Leader (for lately he had begun to call Napoleon "Leader") to live in a house instead of a simple sty（猪圈）. Nevertheless, some animals were worried when they heard the pigs not only ate in the kitchen and used the sitting room, but also slept in the beds.

[P17] Boxer passed it off as usual with "Napoleon is always right!", but Clover thought she remembered a clear rule against beds. She went to the end of the barn（谷仓） and tried to puzzle（谜） out the Seven Commandments（戒律） written there. She could not read more than single letters, so she fetched Muriel. "Muriel," she said, "read me the Fourth Commandment（戒律）. Does it not say something about never sleeping in a bed?" With some difficulty Muriel spelt（拼写） it out. "It says, 'No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets（床单）,'" she announced. Strangely, Clover had not remembered the Fourth Commandment（戒律） mentioning sheets; but it was there on the wall, so it must have.

[P18] Squealer happened to pass by just then, with two or three dogs. He could explain it all. "You have heard then, comrades," he said, "that we pigs now sleep in the beds of the farmhouse? And why not? You did not suppose there was a ruling against beds? A bed merely（仅仅） means a place to sleep in. A pile of straw（稻草） in a stall（畜栏） is a bed. The rule was against sheets, a human invention. We have removed（移开） the sheets from the farmhouse beds, and sleep between blankets（毯子）.

[P19] And they are very comfortable beds too! But we need them, comrades, with all the brainwork（脑力劳动） we must do now. You would not take away our rest, would you? Surely none of you wants Jones back?" The animals told him they were sure at once, and no more was said about the pigs sleeping in the farmhouse beds. And some days later, when it was said the pigs would get up an hour later than the others, no one complained either. By the autumn the animals were tired but happy.

[P20] They had had a hard year, and after they sold part of the hay and corn, the food stores for the winter were not too plentiful（丰富）, but the windmill made up for everything. It was almost half built now. After the harvest there was a long stretch（伸展） of clear dry weather, and the animals worked harder than ever, thinking it well worth while to plod（跋涉） to and fro（来回） all day with blocks of stone if by doing so they could raise the walls another foot. Boxer would even come out at nights and work for an hour or two on his own by the light of the harvest moon. In their spare moments the animals would walk round the half-finished mill（磨坊）, admiring the strength and uprightness（正直） of its walls.

[P21] Only old Benjamin would not get excited about the windmill. As usual, he said nothing more than his strange words that donkeys live a long time. November came, with strong south-west winds. Building had to stop because it was too wet to mix the cement. Then one night the wind was so strong that the farm buildings shook, and some tiles（瓦片） blew off the roof of the barn. The hens woke up screaming in fear because they had all dreamed at the same time of a gun going off far away.

[P22] In the morning the animals came out and found the flagstaff（旗杆） blown down. An elm（榆树） tree at the foot of the orchard（果园） had been pulled up like a radish（萝卜）. Then a cry of despair（绝望） came from every animal. The windmill was in ruins（废墟）. They ran down to the spot（地点）. Napoleon, who seldom walked fast, raced ahead. There it lay, the fruit of all their struggles（斗争）, flat to its foundations（地基）. The stones they had broken and carried were scattered（散落） all around.

[P23] At first they could not speak. They stood and looked sadly at the fallen stone. Napoleon walked to and fro without a word, sometimes snuffing（嗅） at the ground. His tail had grown stiff and twitched（抽搐） sharply（尖锐地）, a sign of great thinking in him. Suddenly he stopped, as if his mind were made up. "Comrades," he said quietly, "do you know who is responsible for this? Do you know the enemy who came in the night and threw down our windmill? SNOWBALL!" he suddenly roared（吼叫） in a voice of thunder. "Snowball has done this thing! Out of pure evil, hoping to set back our plans and avenge（复仇） himself for his shameful（可耻） expulsion（驱逐）, this traitor crept（爬行） here under cover of night and destroyed our work of nearly a year.

[P24] Comrades, I now sentence Snowball to death. 'Animal Hero, Second Class,' and half a bushel（蒲式耳） of apples to any animal who brings him to justice. A full bushel to anyone who catches him alive!" The animals were shocked that Snowball could do such a thing. They cried out in anger and began to plan how to catch him if he came back. Soon a pig's footprints（脚印） were found in the grass near the hill. They led a few yards to a hole in the hedge（树篱）.

[P25] Napoleon smelled them for a long time and said they were Snowball's. He thought Snowball had come from Foxwood（狐林） Farm. "No more waiting, comrades!" cried Napoleon after they looked at the footprints. "We have work to do. This morning we start rebuilding the windmill, and we will build all winter, rain or shine. We will teach this miserable（悲惨的） traitor that he cannot undo（取消） our work so easily. Remember, comrades, our plans must not change: they shall be carried out to the day. Forward, comrades! Long live the windmill!

[P26] Long live Animal Farm!
